subject: Tricky dataset & whether pcountOpen is appropriate framework

messages.author: 09570c3cdd137595
messages.subject: Tricky dataset & whether pcountOpen is appropriate framework
parts:
Hi all,

I am currently working with a bit of a tricky dataset and am wondering more broadly if the open population N-mixture approach (i.e. Dail & Madsen 2011) is the right way to go. I have a lot of experience with occupancy models, but this is my first foray into the N-mixture world.

The dataset comprises three years of nightly acoustic recordings of bats outside a hibernaculum during spring emergence. There are 12 detectors, and the first "hump" of bat calls during emergence takes place over ~12 nights in each year. The goal of this project is to answer "What habitat features are bats using as they emerge from the hibernaculum?" (and, more broadly, how can this information to be used to assist recovery from white-nose syndrome). 

The number of bats on the landscape changes daily -- bats emerge from the hibernaculum, use the immediate landscape around the hibernaculum (where the detector array is located), and then disperse to maternity colonies -- so this is clearly an open population. Detection will vary by temperature and, to a lesser extent, other weather-related variables such as relative humidity, wind speed, precipitation, etc. I was planning to apply pcountOpen to each year separately, using 12 replicates (nightly counts over 12 nights) at 12 sites (detectors). I know our sample size is low.

My two questions are:

(1) Will modeling covariates on gamma (ie "immigration," the number of bats entering the landscape daily) be the key to answering our question about what habitat features bats are using? I was thinking (as the number of calls is hump-shaped over time) gamma could be modeled as 

julianday + julianday^2 + lidarmeasure1 + lidarmeasure2 + ....

(2) Double-counting of bats is almost certain due to the detectors recording all night long & an inability to identify individual bats on the detectors. I know this is a major assumption of N-mixture models and that traditional GOF models will fail to pick up on even the slightest of violations. A counterargument from my collaborators is that bias on N doesn't matter, as we aren't interested in abundance estimation but rather use of habitat features by incoming bats. How slippery is this slope?

Any advice appreciated from those with more experience with this class of models. My thanks in advance for your time and attention.

Best,
Lisanne
